I had the opportunity of discussing this in an open manner with leading academics in China in 2000. It was really enlightning. They view China, with a population of well over 1bn to be too large and too diversified for democracy to make sense. Western style democracy would especially be detrimental to small, remote, less influential regions. So while such a process would be more democratic, the outcome would be less democratic.

What they did believe in, however, is increasing the influence of the people on a local level. Many of these districts are far larger by population than leading nations. But they are, they said, experiencing more transfer of power from Beijing to the provinces, especially those provinces that are well governed, economically successful and with an educated populous. As an example they highlighted that the district we were in (we were in Shanghai) is mainly controlled locally, by people elected locally.

Some of us pushed back and said even the local candidates are pre-vetted by the communist party in Beijing. They laughed and asked "is this any worse than the US system where the candidates are pre-selected by large businesses or a few wealthy donors? I think not, because at least our pre-vetting is based on what we believe is best for the nation, best for good governance, best for the people - unlike in the US where it is often based on what is best for the very wealthy or best for the large companies."

Pretty interesting discussion, and made me less dogmatic in my views.
